claim: Human spermatozoa have to find and maintain the right swimming direction over distances that may exceed their head-to-tail length (~100 μm) by a 1000-fold during their journey from ejaculation to fertilisation.
source: During their journey from ejaculation to fertilisation, human spermatozoa have to find and maintain the right swimming direction over distances that may exceed their head-to-tail length (∼100 μm) by a 1000-fold.
evidence: This is a statement about the biological challenge faced by sperm cells, drawing from established knowledge about mammalian reproduction.

claim: Chemotactic sensing is assumed to provide important guidance in the immediate vicinity of the ovum.
source: Whilst chemotactic sensing (Kaupp et al., 2008) is assumed to provide important guidance in the immediate vicinity of the ovum (Spehr et al., 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Kaupp et al., 2008; Spehr et al., 2003).

claim: It is not known which biochemical or physical mechanisms keep the sperm cells on track as they pass through the cervix, uterus, and oviduct.
source: it is not known which biochemical (Brenker et al., 2012) or physical mechanisms (Winet et al., 1984) keep the sperm cells on track as they pass through the rugged landscapes of cervix, uterus, and oviduct (Katz et al., 2005; Eisenbach and Giojalas, 2006; Suarez and Pacey, 2006).
evidence: This claim identifies a gap in current scientific knowledge, supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Both human and bull spermatozoa swim upstream on spiral-shaped trajectories along the walls of a cylindrical channel.
source: These measurements revealed the interesting result that both human and bull spermatozoa do not simply align against the flow, but instead swim upstream on spiral-shaped trajectories along the walls of a cylindrical channel (Figure 1A; and Video 1).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1A and Video 1.

claim: The transversal velocity component of sperm can be attributed to the chirality of the flagellar beat.
source: The previously unrecognised transversal velocity component can be attributed to the chirality of the flagellar beat.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations and theoretical analysis.

claim: Rheotaxis can help sperm to navigate their way through the oviduct and find the egg cell.
source: The resulting helical swimming patterns enable the spermatozoa to explore collectively the full surface of a cylindrical channel, suggesting that rheotaxis can help sperm to navigate their way through the oviduct and find the egg cell (Miki and Clapham, 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the biological function of rheotaxis, supported by citation and inference from experimental data.

claim: Weak fluid flows can be beneficial to the reproduction of red abalone organisms.
source: Recent experiments on red abalone (Riffell and Zimmer, 2007; Zimmer and Riffell, 2011), a large marine snail that fertilises externally, showed that weak fluid flows can be beneficial to the reproduction of these organisms
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous experimental work on red abalone.

claim: Shear flows could have acted as a selective pressure in gamete evolution.
source: Recent experiments on red abalone (Riffell and Zimmer, 2007; Zimmer and Riffell, 2011), a large marine snail that fertilises externally, showed that weak fluid flows can be beneficial to the reproduction of these organisms, suggesting that shear flows could have acted as a selective pressure in gamete evolution.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about evolutionary pressures, inferred from experimental observations on red abalone.

claim: It is unlikely that local chemotactic gradients steer sperm cells during the initial and intermediate stages of the sexual reproduction process due to complex uterine and oviduct topography and large travelling distances.
source: The complex uterine and oviduct topography (Suarez and Pacey, 2006) and large travelling distances render it unlikely that local chemotactic gradients steer sperm cells during the initial and intermediate stages of the sexual reproduction process.
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical knowledge and cited literature about reproductive tract topography.

claim: Experimental evidence suggests that rapid sperm transport right after insemination is supported by peristaltic pumping driven by muscular contractions of the uterus.
source: Experimental evidence (Kunz et al., 1996) suggests that rapid sperm transport right after insemination is supported by peristaltic pumping driven by muscular contractions of the uterus
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to experimental evidence.

claim: It is not known how sperm navigate in the oviduct.
source: but it is not known how sperm navigate in the oviduct.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current scientific knowledge.

claim: Thermotaxis was proposed as a possible long-range rectification mechanism of sperm swimming in rabbits.
source: Thermotaxis, the directed response of sperm to local temperature differences, was proposed as a possible long-range rectification mechanism of sperm swimming in rabbits (Bahat et al., 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Thermotaxis was recently questioned as it is likely to be inhibited by convective currents that form in the presence of temperature gradients.
source: but recently questioned (Miki and Clapham, 2013) as it is likely to be inhibited by convective currents that form in the presence of temperature gradients.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and involves inference about physical mechanisms.

claim: Mammalian sperm are capable of performing rheotaxis by aligning against a surrounding flow, similar to bacteria and algae.
source: On the other hand, it has long been known that, similar to bacteria (Marcos et al., 2012) and algae (Chengala et al., 2013), mammalian sperm (Adolphi, 1905; Roberts, 1970) are capable of performing rheotaxis, by aligning against a surrounding flow (Marcos et al., 2012; Miki and Clapham, 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to historical and recent research.

claim: Rheotaxis in mammalian sperm has yet to be systematically quantified in experiments.
source: but this effect has yet to be systematically quantified in experiments (Fauci and Dillon, 2006; Suarez and Pacey, 2006).
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature, supported by citations.

claim: It is not known at present how sperm cells respond to variations in shear rate and viscosity.
source: Specifically, it is not known at present how sperm cells respond to variations in shear rate and viscosity, and how long they need to adapt to temporal changes in the flow direction.
evidence: This identifies specific gaps in current knowledge.

claim: It is not known how long sperm cells need to adapt to temporal changes in the flow direction.
source: Specifically, it is not known at present how sperm cells respond to variations in shear rate and viscosity, and how long they need to adapt to temporal changes in the flow direction.
evidence: This identifies a specific gap in current knowledge.

claim: Experiments were performed with viscosities up to μ = 20 mPa·s which is roughly 10× the viscosity of natural seminal fluid.
source: varying systematically shear rates γ˙ and viscosities μ through the physiologically and rheotactically relevant regime, up to μ = 20 mPa·s which is roughly 10× the viscosity of natural seminal fluid (Owen and Katz, 2005).
evidence: This describes experimental parameters and compares them to physiological values cited from literature.

claim: Even in the absence of flow, sperm cells tend to accumulate at surfaces due to a combination of steric repulsion and hydrodynamic forces.
source: Even in the absence of flow, sperm cells tend to accummulate at surfaces (Rothschild, 1963; Denissenko et al., 2012) due to a combination of steric repulsion (Kantsler et al., 2013) and hydrodynamic forces (Fauci and McDonald, 1995; Elgeti et al., 2010; Friedrich et al., 2010; Gaffney et al., 2011; Montenegro-Johnson et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The flagellar beat traces out a cone which, upon collision, aligns with a solid surface, so that the sperm's propulsion vector points into the boundary and the cells become effectively trapped at the surface.
source: This can be explained by the fact that, in essence, the flagellar beat traces out a cone which, upon collision, aligns with a solid surface, so that the sperm's propulsion vector points into the boundary and the cells become effectively trapped at the surface (Kantsler et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an explanation of a physical mechanism, supported by citation.

claim: Both human and bull sperm exhibit optimal upstream swimming at rescaled flow speeds u20 ∼ 1.
source: The results for the upstream velocity reveal that both human and bull sperm exhibit optimal upstream swimming at rescaled flow speeds u20 ∼ 1
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: There is an optimal shear regime for the rectification of sperm swimming.
source: implying that there is an optimal shear regime for the rectification of sperm swimming.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing optimal upstream swimming at specific flow speeds.

claim: At low viscosities (μ ≪10 mPa·s), human spermatozoa exhibit a substantial shear-induced transverse velocity component that becomes suppressed at very high viscosities.
source: Remarkably, however, we also find that, at low viscosities (μ ≪10 mPa·s), human spermatozoa exhibit a substantial shear-induced transverse velocity component that becomes suppressed at very high viscosities.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental measurements.

claim: For bull spermatozoa, the mean transverse component is generally weaker and less sensitive to viscosity variations compared to human sperm.
source: By contrast, for bull spermatozoa, the mean transverse component is generally weaker and less sensitive to viscosity variations.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental measurements comparing bull and human sperm.

claim: Once a sperm cell has become trapped at a surface, its tail explores, on average, regions of higher flow velocity than the head, resulting in a net torque that turns the head against the flow.
source: Once a sperm cell has become trapped at a surface, its tail explores, on average, regions of higher flow velocity than the head, resulting in a net torque that turns the head against the flow (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an explanation of the physical mechanism, illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: If the shear velocity is too low, the orientational 'noise' inhibits upstream swimming.
source: If the shear velocity is too low the orientational 'noise', which is caused by a combination of intrinsic fluctuations in the cells' swimming apparatus, thermal fluctuations, and elastohydrodynamic effects, inhibits upstream swimming
evidence: This is an inference about the physical mechanism explaining the experimental observations.

claim: If the shear velocity becomes too large, the sperm will simply be advected downstream by the flow.
source: whereas if the shear velocity becomes too large the sperm will simply be advected downstream by the flow
evidence: This is an inference about the physical mechanism based on fluid dynamics principles.

claim: There exists an optimal intermediate shear rate for upstream swimming.
source: implying that there exists an optimal intermediate shear rate for upstream swimming.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations and physical reasoning.

claim: The maximum of the upstream velocity decreases more strongly with viscosity for bull sperm than for human sperm.
source: Interestingly, we find that the maximum of the upstream velocity decreases more strongly with viscosity for bull sperm than for human sperm (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Differences in cell morphology can substantially alter swimming behavior, as suggested by previous numerical studies for bacterial cells.
source: This could be due to differences in cell morphology, as previous numerical studies (Smith et al., 2011) for bacterial cells suggest that differences in head shape can substantially alter swimming behavior.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous numerical studies.

claim: Bull sperm have a flatter head than human sperm.
source: Bull sperm have a flatter head than human sperm
evidence: This is a statement about morphological differences based on established biological knowledge.

claim: The flatter head of bull sperm likely suppresses the rotational motion of the cell at high viscosities, leading to an effectively smaller vertical beat amplitude A.
source: which likely suppresses the rotational motion of the cell at high viscosities thus leading to an effectively smaller vertical beat amplitude A.
evidence: This is an inference about the physical mechanism based on morphological differences.

claim: At high values of μ, the tail beat of bull sperm becomes essentially two-dimensional and constricted to the vicinity of the surface.
source: This could explain why, at high values of μ, the tail beat of bull sperm becomes essentially two-dimensional and constricted to the vicinity of the surface
evidence: This is an inference drawn from experimental observations and physical reasoning.

claim: When the tail beat becomes two-dimensional and constricted to the surface, alignment against the flow becomes less efficient.
source: so that alignment against the flow becomes less efficient.
evidence: This is an inference about the physical mechanism.

claim: Sperm of invertebrae and mammals are known to exhibit different chiral beat patterns depending on environmental conditions.
source: To understand the unexpectedly strong transverse velocity component of human sperm at μ ≲5 mPa·s, as typical of the seminal fluid (Owen and Katz, 2005), it is important to recall that sperm of invertebrae and mammals are known to exhibit different chiral beat patterns depending on environmental conditions (Gibbons, 1982; Ishijima and Hamaguchi, 1993; Woolley and Vernon, 2001; Smith et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Shear flows are capable of separating particles along the transverse direction according to their chirality.
source: and that shear flows are capable of separating particles along the transverse direction according to their chirality (Marcos et al., 2009; Talkner et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Human sperm exhibit a strong helical beat component at low-to-moderate values of μ.
source: Human sperm exhibit a strong helical beat component at low-to-moderate values of μ (Video 2)
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Video 2.

claim: The chirality of human sperm beat becomes suppressed at high viscosities, resulting in more planar wave forms.
source: but this chirality becomes suppressed at high viscosities (Video 3) resulting in more planar wave forms (Smith et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations in Video 3 and citation to previous research.

claim: The beat of a bull sperm flagellum is more similar to a rigidly rotating planar wave even at low viscosities.
source: For comparison, the beat of a bull sperm flagellum is more similar to a rigidly rotating planar wave even at low viscosities (Video 4)
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Video 4.

claim: Bull sperm exhibit weaker chirality leading to smaller transverse velocities compared to human sperm.
source: thus exhibiting a weaker chirality and leading to smaller transverse velocities (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is an inference from experimental observations shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The flagellar beating pattern can be controlled not only by viscosity but also by changes in calcium concentration.
source: Since the flagellar beating pattern can be controlled not only by viscosity but also by changes in calcium concentration (Ishijima and Hamaguchi, 1993)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Higher organisms appear to possess several means for tuning transverse and upstream swimming of sperm.
source: higher organisms appear to possess several means for tuning transverse and upstream swimming of sperm.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed effects of viscosity and calcium concentration on flagellar beating.

claim: Sperm cells are exposed to temporally varying flows driven by uterine contractions in addition to typically outward directed mucus flow in the oviduct.
source: In addition to typically outward directed mucus flow in the oviduct, sperm cells are also exposed to temporally varying flows driven by uterine contractions (Fauci and Dillon, 2006; Suarez and Pacey, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Upon flow reversal, a sperm cell typically performs a U-turn.
source: Upon flow reversal, a sperm cell typically performs a U-turn (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: The characteristic radius of curvature of the trajectory and the typical turning time τ were found to increase strongly with viscosity.
source: The characteristic radius of curvature of the trajectory and the typical turning time τ were found to increase strongly with viscosity.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental measurements.

claim: At low viscosity (μ ∼ 1 mPa·s), sperm realign rapidly against the new flow direction with a typical response time of τ ∼ 5 s to 10 s.
source: At low viscosity, μ ∼ 1 mPa·s, sperm realign rapidly against the new flow direction with a typical response time of τ ∼ 5 s to 10 s
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental measurements.

claim: At low viscosity, the curvature radius of sperm U-turns is of the order of one or two sperm lengths ℓ ∼ 60 μm.
source: and the curvature radius is of the order of one or two sperm lengths ℓ ∼ 60 μm (Video 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental measurements shown in Video 5.

claim: At a larger viscosity of μ ∼ 12 mPa·s, both curvature radius and response time increase by approximately a factor of 5 compared to low viscosity.
source: By contrast, at a larger viscosity of μ ∼ 12 mPa·s, which is roughly 4× higher than the natural viscosity of the ejaculate, both curvature radius and response time increase by approximately a factor of 5 (Video 6).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental measurements shown in Video 6.

claim: The response times of sperm to flow reversal are of the order of typical cervical contractions.
source: Interestingly, these response times are of the order of typical cervical contractions (Kunz et al., 1996)
evidence: This is a comparison between experimental findings and physiological data from cited literature.

claim: There is a possible fine-tuning between muscular activity of the uterus and turning behavior of sperm cells.
source: suggesting a possible fine-tuning between muscular activity of the uterus and turning behavior of sperm cells.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the similarity between response times and contraction periods.

claim: Immediately after flow reversal, sperm orientation and flow direction point for a short period of time in approximately the same direction, leading to a momentarily increased transport velocity.
source: In particular, immediately after the flow reversal, sperm orientation and flow direction point for a short period of time in approximately the same direction, leading to a momentarily increased transport velocity (see velocity peaks in Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2C.

claim: By switching flow directions back and forth at an optimal rate, the transport efficiency of an initially rectified sperm population can be enhanced.
source: Thus, by switching flow directions back and forth at an optimal rate, the transport efficiency of an initially rectified sperm population can be enhanced.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed velocity peaks after flow reversal.

claim: Resistive force theory was used to infer a minimal mathematical model that incorporates the main physical mechanisms.
source: To test whether our understanding of the experimental observations is correct and to provide a basis for future theoretical studies, we used resistive force theory to infer a minimal mathematical model that incorporates the main physical mechanisms discussed above (details are provided in the Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the theoretical approach used in the study.

claim: The model assumes that the effective two-dimensional motion of a sperm cell swimming close to a surface in the presence of a shear flow can be described in terms of its position vector R(t) and its orientation unit vector N(t).
source: The model assumes that the effective two-dimensional motion of a sperm cell, that swims close to a surface in the presence of a shear flow can be described in terms of its position vector R(t) = (X(t),Y(t)) and its orientation unit vector N(t) = (Nx(t),Ny(t)).
evidence: This describes the assumptions of the mathematical model.

claim: The model was obtained by approximating the flagellum by a rigid conical helix.
source: Equations 1 and 2 were obtained by approximating the flagellum by a rigid conical helix, with the polar geometry of the enveloping cone dictating the mathematical structure of the deterministic turning terms (see Supplementary file 1 for details of the calculation).
evidence: This describes the approximation used in deriving the mathematical model.

claim: The minimal model does not accurately capture the dynamics of individual cells at zero shear due to simplifying assumptions.
source: The simplifying assumptions underlying Equations 1 and 2 imply that this minimal model does not accurately capture the dynamics of individual cells at zero shear, as the deterministic terms in Equation 2 neglect the intrinsic curvature of cell trajectories.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the model.

claim: When analyzing the in-plane curvature for a large number of human sperm trajectories at zero shear, a broad distribution of curvatures with a small positive mean curvature of (5.6 ± 1.3)·10−4 μm was found at low viscosity (1 mPa·s).
source: However, when analyzing the in-plane curvature for a large number of human sperm trajectories (>100,000 sample points from more than 1200 cells) at zero shear, we found a broad distribution of curvatures with a small positive mean curvature of (5.6 ± 1.3)·10−4 μm at low viscosity (1 mPa·s)
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: At high viscosity (12 mPa·s), human sperm trajectories showed a small negative mean curvature (−1.9 ± 0.1)·10−3 μm at zero shear.
source: and a small negative mean curvature (−1.9 ± 0.1)·10−3 μm at high viscosity (12 mPa·s)
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The different signs of mean curvature at different viscosities are consistent with the observed change in the transverse velocity for human sperm at high viscosity.
source: where the different signs are consistent with the observed change in the transverse velocity for human sperm at high viscosity (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is an inference connecting curvature measurements to velocity observations.

claim: Values α∈[0.2, 0.4], β∈[0.05, 0.1] and D∈[0.2, 0.3] rad/s yield good quantitative agreement with the experimental results for both stationary flow and flow reversal.
source: By performing systematic parameter scans, we found that values α∈[0.2, 0.4], β∈[0.05, 0.1] and D∈[0.2, 0.3] rad/s yield good quantitative agreement with the experimental results for both stationary flow (Figure 3A) and flow reversal (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is a finding from the model parameter fitting to experimental data.

claim: The coupling between shear flow and beat chirality dominates the transverse velocity dynamics.
source: suggesting that the coupling between shear flow and beat chirality dominates the transverse velocity dynamics.
evidence: This is an inference from the model parameter fitting results.

claim: Despite some strong simplifications, the effects included in the model capture the main physical mechanisms relevant for understanding sperm motion in shear flow near a surface.
source: We may therefore conclude that, despite some strong simplifications, the effects included in the model capture indeed the main physical mechanisms relevant for understanding sperm motion in shear flow near a surface.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the agreement between model predictions and experimental data.

claim: Upstream swimming of mammalian sperm due to rheotaxis is more complex than previously thought.
source: Our experimental results show that upstream swimming of mammalian sperm due to rheotaxis is more complex than previously thought.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Human sperm cells exhibit a significant transverse velocity component that could be of relevance in the fertilisation process.
source: Human sperm cells were found to exhibit a significant transverse velocity component that could be of relevance in the fertilisation process
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments with speculation about biological relevance.

claim: The spiralling motion enables spermatozoa to explore collectively a larger surface area of the oviducts, thereby increasing the probability of locating egg cells.
source: as the ensuing spiralling motion enables spermatozoa to explore collectively a larger surface area of the oviducts, thereby increasing the probability of locating egg cells.
evidence: This is an inference about the biological function of the observed spiralling motion.

claim: The transverse velocity component arises from a preferred handedness in the flagella beat in the presence of shear flow.
source: Our theoretical analysis implies that the transverse velocity component arises from a preferred handedness in the flagella beat in the presence of shear flow
evidence: This is a conclusion from the theoretical analysis.

claim: The findings for mammalian sperm contrast with recent findings for male microgametes of the malaria parasite Plasmodium berghei.
source: in contrast to recent findings for male microgametes of the malaria parasite Plasmodium berghei (Wilson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison with cited research on a different organism.

claim: The data provide substantial statistical evidence for the hypothesis that mammalian sperm have evolved to achieve optimal upstream swimming near surfaces.
source: Due to the large sample size, our data provide substantial statistical evidence for the hypothesis that mammalian sperm have evolved to achieve optimal upstream swimming near surfaces
evidence: This is a speculative claim about evolution supported by the large dataset.

claim: Sperm may be exploiting the enhanced fluid production in the female reproductive system during the fertile phase and after intercourse.
source: possibly exploiting the enhanced fluid production in the female reproductive system during the fertile phase (Eschenbach et al., 2000) and after intercourse (Miki and Clapham, 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about biological function, supported by citations.

claim: The improved quantitative knowledge may help to design more efficient artificial insemination strategies.
source: The improved quantitative knowledge derived from this data may help to design more efficient artificial insemination strategies, for example, by optimising the viscosity and chemical composition of fertilisation media and adjusting injection techniques to maximise upstream swimming of sperm cells.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential applications of the research.

claim: The results yield a cohesive picture of the mechanistic and fluid-mechanical aspects of long-distance sperm navigation when combined with recent measurements on flagella-mediated contact interactions.
source: Combined with recent measurements (Kantsler et al., 2013), which clarified the importance of flagella-mediated contact interactions for the accumulation of sperm cells at surfaces, the results presented here yield a cohesive picture of the mechanistic and fluid-mechanical (Friedrich et al., 2010) aspects of long-distance sperm navigation.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the current findings with previous research, supported by citations.

claim: Future work should focus on merging these insights with quantitative studies of chemotaxis to obtain a differentiated understanding of the interplay between physical and chemical factors during various stages of the mammalian reproduction process.
source: Future work should focus on merging these insights with quantitative studies of chemotaxis (Spehr et al., 2003; Kaupp et al., 2008; Zimmer and Riffell, 2011; Brenker et al., 2012) to obtain a differentiated understanding of the interplay between physical and chemical factors during various stages of the mammalian reproduction process.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research, supported by citations to relevant work.

claim: Cryogenically frozen bull spermatozoa were purchased from Genus Breeding.
source: Cryogenically frozen bull spermatozoa were purchased from Genus Breeding.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about sample sourcing.

claim: Human samples from healthy undisclosed normozoospermic donors were obtained from Bourn Hall Clinic.
source: Human samples from healthy undisclosed normozoospermic donors were obtained from Bourn Hall Clinic.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about sample sourcing.

claim: Donors provided informed consent in accordance with the regulations of The University of Cambridge Human Biology Research Ethics Committee.
source: Donors provided informed consent in accordance with the regulations of The University of Cambridge Human Biology Research Ethics Committee.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical compliance.

claim: The absence of circular trajectories at zero-shear implies that the sperm are capacitated.
source: The absence of circular trajectories at zero-shear implies that the sperm are capacitated (Miki and Clapham, 2013).
evidence: This is an inference from experimental observations, supported by citation.

claim: The measured velocity profile is found identical to the calculated values from solving the Stokes equations for the given geometry.
source: The measured velocity profile is found identical to the calculated values from solving the Stokes equations for the given geometry.
evidence: This is a validation of the experimental setup against theoretical predictions.

claim: The sample size in a single experiment exceeds 100,000 velocity vectors.
source: The sample size in a single experiment exceeds 100,000 velocity vectors
evidence: This is a statement about the statistical power of the experiments.

claim: Each measurement for a given viscosity and shear rate was repeated a few times with different sperm samples.
source: each measurement for a given viscosity and a shear rate was repeated a few times with different sperm samples.
evidence: This is a statement about experimental reproducibility.

claim: The interplay of fluid shear, steric surface-interactions, and chirality of the flagellar beat leads to stable upstream spiralling motion of sperm cells.
source: Our measurements show that the interplay of fluid shear, steric surface-interactions, and chirality of the flagellar beat leads to stable upstream spiralling motion of sperm cells
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental measurements.

claim: The upstream spiralling motion provides a generic and robust rectification mechanism to support mammalian fertilisation.
source: thus providing a generic and robust rectification mechanism to support mammalian fertilisation.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the biological function of the observed behavior.

claim: A minimal mathematical model is presented that accounts quantitatively for the experimental observations.
source: A minimal mathematical model is presented that accounts quantitatively for the experimental observations.
evidence: This is a statement about the theoretical contribution of the study.
